fields.foundation: The Neo-Sumerian Empire, also known as the Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III), arose around 2112 BCE, after the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and the political fragmentation that followed in Mesopotamia. Utu-hegal of Uruk expelled the Gutian rulers who had dominated parts of the south. Ur-Nammu, who governed Ur under Utu-hegal and may have been his kinsman, soon took power in his own right and founded a new dynasty. The collapse of Akkadian central control and the instability that followed had created conditions favourable to a new centralised power. Ur-Nammu consolidated control over Sumerian cities such as Uruk, Lagash and Nippur and re-established Sumerian political and cultural pre-eminence after a period of foreign domination. His reign deliberately revived Sumerian traditions in language, religion and administration. His son Shulgi (r. c. 2094–2047 BCE) expanded and centralised the state, making it one of the most bureaucratically organised empires of the ancient Near East.
fields.socioeconomy: The economy of the Neo-Sumerian Empire was centralised and managed by institutions: it was a redistributive system dominated by temple and palace households. Agriculture was its basis. Extensive irrigation networks drawing on the Tigris and Euphrates allowed the cultivation of barley, dates and other staples. Land was largely controlled by the crown, the temples and elite officials, and labour was organised through dependent workers, including free peasants, temple personnel and enslaved individuals, who were often paid in rations of barley, oil and wool. The administration recorded economic activity in close detail on cuneiform tablets, tens of thousands of which survive from sites such as Umma, Girsu and Puzrish-Dagan, the great livestock collection centre near Nippur. Textile production, metalwork and other crafts were organised in institutional workshops, while long-distance trade brought timber, metals and stone from regions such as the Iranian plateau and the Persian Gulf. Taxation and labour obligations, among them the rotating provincial contributions known as bala, kept resources flowing to the central authority, which redistributed goods to sustain administrative, religious and military functions.
fields.military: The army of the Neo-Sumerian Empire was a structured force supported by the state. It defended the heartland and projected power into the surrounding highlands. Armies consisted largely of infantry equipped with spears, shields and helmets, organised under a central command in keeping with the bureaucratic character of the state. The empire inherited and refined earlier Mesopotamian practices, including the use of fortified cities and defensive walls to secure the main urban centres. Under Shulgi, the army campaigned repeatedly in the Zagros against peoples such as the Lullubi and the city of Simurrum, while Susa and parts of Elam were brought under Ur’s control. Soldiers received rations and, in some cases, land allocations in exchange for service, and frontier provinces were placed under military governors. As Amorite pressure mounted, Shu-Sin built a long fortification wall, known as the Amorite Wall or the “Repeller of the Tidnum”, to protect the heartland. Despite these measures, the army could not contain sustained external pressure in the empire’s final decades.
fields.governance: The Neo-Sumerian Empire was governed through an advanced bureaucracy that kept tight control over economic and administrative life. From Shulgi onwards, the kings were deified during their lifetimes, and religious ideology and close association with the major temples legitimised their authority. The Code of Ur-Nammu, traditionally attributed to the dynasty’s founder though possibly issued by Shulgi, is the oldest surviving law code. It set out penalties concerning justice, property and social relations, many of them monetary fines. The core of the empire was divided into provinces administered by civilian governors (ensi), while separate military governors oversaw the frontier zones, all accountable to the central administration. Extensive record-keeping, the work of scribes, gave the state oversight of taxation, labour and resource distribution. The use of the Sumerian language in official documentation reinforced cultural continuity, while standardised weights, measures and calendars supported efficient government. This organisation enabled the state to manage a complex society but also made it heavily dependent on central coordination.
fields.impact: The Neo-Sumerian Empire influenced the political and cultural development of Mesopotamia and the wider ancient Near East. It revived Sumerian identity, preserving linguistic, religious and administrative practices at a time when Akkadian and Amorite speakers were increasingly prominent. Its bureaucratic innovations, including systematic record-keeping and centralised economic management, influenced later Mesopotamian states, particularly the kingdom of Babylon. Its legal tradition, represented by the Code of Ur-Nammu, established precedents for later codes, including that of Hammurabi. Royal hymns and literary works composed or patronised at the Ur III court were copied by scribes of the Old Babylonian period, and much of Sumerian literature survives as a result. The empire also sustained trade networks connecting Mesopotamia with surrounding regions. Its monumental architecture, above all the great ziggurat of Ur begun by Ur-Nammu, expressed religious devotion and political authority, and reinforced Mesopotamia’s position as a centre of early urban civilisation.
fields.decline: The decline of the Neo-Sumerian Empire set in under Shulgi’s successors, as internal and external pressures strained the state’s administrative and military capacities. The centralised system was efficient but vulnerable to disruption, particularly as provincial governors asserted their autonomy during the reign of the last king, Ibbi-Sin. Environmental factors, including possible salinisation of farmland, may have reduced productivity, and surviving correspondence records grain shortages and soaring prices. Amorite incursions from the west disrupted communications and agriculture, and the defensive wall built against them proved ineffective. Ishbi-Erra, an official sent to procure grain, established an independent power base at Isin, while in the east Elam and the highland state of Shimashki broke free of Ur’s control. Around 2004 BCE, Elamite forces captured and sacked Ur and carried Ibbi-Sin into captivity in Anshan, bringing the empire to an end. A period of fragmentation followed, in which rival dynasties, among them the Isin and Larsa dynasties, contended for supremacy.
fields.summary: The Neo-Sumerian Empire is an early example of state centralisation, and its administration and cultural revival influenced the later development of Mesopotamian civilisation.
fields.teaser: The Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III) was a Sumerian renaissance, with an elaborate bureaucratic state and monumental ziggurats including the great Ziggurat of Ur.
fields.t0: The Neo-Sumerian Empire, or Third Dynasty of Ur, revived Sumerian rule in southern Mesopotamia after the Akkadian collapse.
fields.t1: Its bureaucracy recorded the economy on tens of thousands of tablets, and its law code is the oldest that survives.
fields.t2: Amorite incursions, grain shortages and breakaway governors weakened it until Elam sacked Ur c. 2004 BCE.
fields.dyk: The Code of Ur-Nammu, some three centuries older than Hammurabi's, punished many offences with monetary fines rather than physical penalties.
